Chapter Two: The Four Core Types of Regret
As you look back on your life, have you ever noticed certain regrets seem to pop up more than others? Even though our experiences are unique, regret tends to follow a few familiar patterns. When you understand these patterns, regret feels a little less overwhelming—and a lot more useful.
Let’s start with the most basic kind: regrets about the foundations of life. Think of these as the building blocks—your health, your education, your finances. Imagine a man in his fifties, sitting in a doctor’s office, wishing he’d taken better care of himself. Or picture a woman staring at her savings account, wondering why she never learned to budget. These aren’t regrets about one big moment. Instead, they’re about all those slow, steady choices that add up over time. You can almost hear the voice in their heads: “If only I’d started sooner. If only I’d paid more attention.”
Then there are regrets about boldness. These are the ones that whisper, “What if you’d taken that leap?” Maybe a college student dreamed of studying abroad, but fear kept her home. Years pass, and she still wonders what adventures she missed. Or a man who once thought about starting his own business, but decided it was too risky. Even decades later, the idea lingers in the back of his mind. These regrets aren’t about playing it safe—they’re about the chances you didn’t take, and the longing for a life that might have been just a little more daring.
Now, moral regrets—they hit on a deeper level. These come from the moments when your actions didn’t match your values. Maybe a father remembers the time he lied to a friend, and it still stings. Or a woman recalls cheating on a test back in high school, and even now, she feels that pang of guilt—even if nobody else ever found out. Moral regrets are about wanting to be better, to live with integrity. And because they get right to the heart of who you are, they often carry the heaviest weight.
Finally, there are regrets about connection. These are tied to the people in your life—friendships that faded, family you drifted from, words you never said. Think of a man who hasn’t spoken to his brother in years, wishing he’d reached out. Or a woman who remembers a friend she lost touch with after a misunderstanding, and feels both sadness and longing. These regrets are about missed chances to connect, to heal, or just to say “I care.”
What’s really striking is how these four types—foundation, boldness, moral, and connection—show up in almost everyone’s story. No matter where you come from, they point to what matters most: security, growth, integrity, belonging. When you recognize these patterns, regret isn’t this confusing feeling anymore—it becomes a kind of map, showing you the places in your life that matter most, and where change is truly possible.
Picture a young professional looking back on her twenties. Her biggest regrets aren’t about money or status; they’re about the friendships she let slip away. Or an older man, reflecting on his career, who realizes his deepest regret isn’t a failed project—but a moment when he didn’t stand up for what he believed was right. These moments aren’t just painful—they’re clarifying. They show you where your attention and effort are needed, and where healing can actually begin.
So, here’s the key takeaway: regret isn’t just about the past. It’s a window into what truly matters to you right now. By understanding the core types of regret, you can turn these feelings into a guide—something that helps you move forward, instead of a weight you have to carry.
